corpus_definition: a statement about what the weather will be like.

forms.definition: a report that says what the weather will be like soon
forms.example: The weather forecast says it will rain tomorrow.
forms.note: Also used for money and business: 'a sales forecast'.

syn.note: A general word for saying what will happen; forecast is used most for weather.
Related: the general picture of the weather for the next few days.
Related: a weather report can talk about today, not only the future.

forms.definition: to say what the weather will be like in the future
forms.example: They have forecast snow for the mountains this weekend.
forms.note: Past tense and past participle: forecast or forecasted.

syn.note: Very close; predict is used for anything, not only weather.
Related: to know that something will happen, often a problem.

forms.note: There is no adjective from this word. Use the noun before another noun: 'forecast rain', 'the forecast temperature'.

people.definition: a person whose job is to say what the weather will be
people.example: The forecaster on TV said it will be hot all week.

context.text: Every morning my father watches the weather forecast. Yesterday the forecaster forecast heavy rain in Tashkent, so we all took umbrellas.

reviewer_note: fore- is not in the affix table, so no prefix is claimed; noun and verb are the same spelling.

forms.note: There is no common noun for this quality. For the person, see People & things (foreigner).

forms.definition: coming from or belonging to another country
forms.example: She can speak many foreign languages.

syn.note: Used before a noun for things from far away across the sea: 'overseas students'.
Related: between or involving many countries, not just one other country.
Related but formal and often negative: strange and not familiar.

ant.note: Inside your own country: 'domestic flights' vs 'foreign flights'.
Belonging to the place where you were born: 'native language' vs 'foreign language'.
From this area or town.

forms.note: There is no adverb. Say 'abroad' or 'in another country'.

people.definition: a person who comes from another country
people.example: Many foreigners visit Bukhara in spring.
people.note: Can sound unfriendly; 'visitor' or 'tourist' is often more polite.

context.text: At the market in Samarkand, a foreigner asked me for directions. I was happy to practise a foreign language, so I answered him in English.

reviewer_note: foreigner is a person noun, so it goes in People & things; no noun for the quality is common enough for learners.

corpus_definition: Suitable for serious or official events and occasions.

forms.definition: serious and correct behaviour that follows official rules
forms.example: The formality of the ceremony made the children nervous.
forms.note: The plural 'formalities' means official things you must do: 'passport formalities'.

syn.note: Related: special, serious actions at an official event.
Related: the rules of polite behaviour.

ant.note: A relaxed and friendly way of behaving.

forms.definition: to make a plan or agreement official, often in writing
forms.example: The two companies formalized their agreement last month.
forms.note: Belongs to formal = official and following rules (a formal agreement), not formal clothes or events. British spelling: formalise.

forms.definition: right for serious or official events, not relaxed
forms.example: He wore a formal suit to the meeting.

syn.note: Close for events and letters: 'an official dinner'.
Related, about clothes: neat and nice-looking (British English).
Related: used at a ceremony, like a wedding.
Related, about language: careful and respectful.

ant.note: Relaxed and friendly: 'informal clothes'.
Easy and relaxed, especially clothes: 'casual jeans'.

forms.definition: in a serious and correct way, right for official events
forms.example: The guests were formally dressed for the wedding.

syn.note: Close when talking about events or announcements.
Related: in the correct way.

ant.note: In a relaxed and friendly way.
In a relaxed way, especially about clothes.

context.text: My sister's wedding in Fergana was very formal. All the men were formally dressed in dark suits, and the formality of the evening made my little brother very quiet.

reviewer_note: formalize kept as other_meaning (official agreements). Don't confuse formally with formerly (= before).

corpus_definition: the state of being able to do what you want.

forms.definition: the state of being able to do or say what you want
forms.example: They enjoyed their new freedom after graduation.

syn.note: Very close but more formal, often about the law and politics.
Not needing other people to help or control you.
Related: the chance to decide for yourself.

ant.note: Being kept in a prison or cage.
Being owned by another person and forced to work.

forms.definition: to let a person or animal leave a prison or cage
forms.example: The police freed the man after two days.

syn.note: Very close and common in news.
Formal, often about a country or group of people.
Easy, everyday phrase.

ant.note: To put someone in prison.
To catch a person or animal and keep them.

forms.definition: able to do what you want, not controlled by others
forms.example: After the exams, the students were free to go home.
forms.note: free also means 'costing no money' (a free ticket); that is a different meaning.

syn.note: Not controlled by other people.
Related and formal: with no limits or rules.

ant.note: Kept in a prison or cage.
Limited by rules.

forms.definition: without anyone stopping or controlling you
forms.example: In this park, children can play freely.

syn.note: Related: without hiding anything, especially when speaking.

context.text: After school, I finally had the freedom to choose my own job. Now I am free to travel, and I can freely decide where to live.

reviewer_note: freedom is made from free (free + -dom); -dom is not in the affix table so no affix is claimed for it. The 'costs nothing' meaning of free is only mentioned in a note.

corpus_definition: to bring your eyebrows together to show anger or worry

forms.definition: an angry or worried look with the eyebrows pulled together
forms.example: She looked at the bill with a frown.

syn.note: A stronger, angrier look.
Related: an ugly face you make because of pain or dislike.

ant.note: A happy look with the mouth turned up.

forms.definition: to pull your eyebrows together because you are angry or worried
forms.example: She frowned when she read the unexpected bad news.
forms.note: frown on/upon something means 'disapprove of it', a different meaning.

syn.note: Stronger: to look very angry.
Related: to look at someone angrily for a long time.
Related: to make an ugly face because of pain or dislike.

ant.note: To look happy with the mouth turned up.
To smile widely.

context.text: My teacher frowned when I came late again. I saw the frown on her face and said sorry at once.

reviewer_note: Only the verb and its noun conversion are learner words; frown on (= disapprove) is a separate meaning.

corpus_definition: a place where people go to see art

forms.definition: a building or room where people can look at paintings and other art
forms.example: We spent all afternoon at the art gallery.
forms.note: Plural: galleries. It can also mean the high seats in a theatre, or a set of photos on your phone.

syn.note: Related: a museum shows old or important objects, not only art.
Related: a show of art for a short time; it can be in a gallery.
Related: a room where things such as cars or furniture are shown for sale.

forms.note: There is no adjective. Use the noun before another noun: 'gallery owner', 'gallery visitors'.

context.text: There is a new gallery near our university in Tashkent. Last Saturday my friends and I went to see the paintings there, and the gallery was full of students.

reviewer_note: Single noun with no learner-level derived forms; context uses only the one form.

corpus_definition: to risk money on a game or event hoping to win more

forms.definition: the activity of playing cards or betting money to try to win more
forms.example: Gambling is a dangerous habit for many young people.

syn.note: Very close; betting is often on sports or races.

forms.definition: a risky action that may bring a good result or a bad one
forms.example: Moving to a new city was a big gamble for him.

syn.note: Close: something that could go wrong.
Related: money you risk on a result.

forms.definition: to risk money on a game or a race to try to win more
forms.example: He gambled away all his savings at the casino.
forms.note: Don't confuse with 'gambol' (to jump about happily), which sounds the same.

syn.note: Very close and common in everyday English.
Formal or old-fashioned word for bet.
Related: to do something that could lose you money or cause harm.

forms.note: There is no adjective. Use the noun before another noun: 'a gambling problem'.

people.definition: a person who often risks money on games or races
people.example: The old gambler lost his house playing cards.

context.text: My uncle never gambles because he says gambling only makes people poor. He knew a gambler who lost his car in one night.

reviewer_note: Noun slot leads with gambling (the activity) because the verb meaning is about money; gamble as a noun (a risky action) is an extra.

corpus_definition: Happy to share your money or things with others.

forms.definition: the quality of being happy to give money, time or help to others
forms.example: Thank you for your generosity during the holiday.

syn.note: Related: being nice and helpful, not only about giving things.
Thinking about other people before yourself.
Related: giving money or help to people who need it.

ant.note: Thinking only about yourself.
Not wanting to give or spend money (British English).

forms.definition: happy to give money, time or things to other people
forms.example: He is very generous with his time.
forms.note: It can also mean 'bigger than usual': 'a generous piece of cake'.

syn.note: Related: nice and helpful to others.
Thinking about other people's needs first.
Related: giving to people who are poor or in need.

ant.note: Not wanting to spend or share money (British English).
Thinking only about yourself.
Informal: not wanting to spend money.

forms.definition: in a way that shows you are happy to give to others
forms.example: Local families gave generously to help the school.

syn.note: Related: in a nice and helpful way.
Related: giving without trying to keep things for yourself.

ant.note: Thinking only about yourself.

context.text: My grandmother is the most generous person I know. She always shares her food with neighbours, and everyone in our mahalla talks about her generosity. She gives generously even when she has little.

reviewer_note: -ity in generosity and -ous in generous are not claimed because removing them does not leave a clean English word.

corpus_definition: a very tiny living thing that can cause illness

forms.definition: a very small living thing that can make people ill
forms.example: Wash your hands to stop the spread of germs.

syn.note: Related: a scientific word for some tiny living things; some are good for you.
Related: a very small thing that causes illnesses like flu.
Informal: 'There's a stomach bug going around.'
Scientific word for a tiny living thing.

forms.definition: to start to grow, as a seed does
forms.example: The beans germinated after three days in wet soil.
forms.note: Belongs to germ = the small part of a seed that grows, not the tiny thing that causes illness.
There is no common adjective. Use the noun before another noun: 'germ protection'.

context.text: Our teacher tells us that germs live on door handles and phones. Before lunch, everyone in our class washes their hands with soap to kill the germs.

reviewer_note: germinate is kept as other_meaning (seed sense); compounds like germ-free are left out.

corpus_definition: To have a good and friendly connection with someone.
particle_note: Not separable: 'get on with someone', never 'get someone on with'. Often with 'well': 'I get on well with my brother.' Without an object: 'We get on well.' Mostly British; American English says 'get along with'.

relations.note: Same meaning, more common in American English.
Related: you like someone; get on with is about how you behave together.
To argue with someone and stop being friends.

context.text: I get on well with my new coworkers in the office. My sister doesn't get on with her roommate, so she wants to move.

reviewer_note: get on with also means 'continue doing something' (get on with your work); this map keeps only the friendship meaning.
